Article Title: For every 30 Chinese AI researchers moving to the US, only one went to China; migration expert warns: The danger for the US is...
Article Text:
30 Chinese AI researchers move to US for every 1 going to China: Carnegie study

China now produces more top AI researchers than any other country

A booming home industry and travel curbs are keeping Chinese AI talent at home

South Korea and Singapore are the other big winners in the AI talent race

The US-China race for artificial intelligence is usually measured in chips and frontier models. A new study measures it in people, and the flow still runs heavily one way. For every 30 Chinese-origin AI researchers working in the United States in 2025, only one US-trained researcher was working in China, according to the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. In 2022, that ratio stood at 46 to one.The gap is narrowing, but slowly, and a migration expert says the headline number may be hiding the real problem. "The danger for the U.S. is a slow erosion of its appeal to attract talent that compounds over decades," said Yingyi Ma, a sociology professor at Syracuse University who studies Asian students in America. "By the time the effect shows up in the data, it is hard to reverse."Her point rests on timing. The study tracks where researchers studied and where they work now, but not when they moved. Most made that call years before the Trump administration tightened student visas, added a $100,000 fee to new H-1B petitions and cut federal research funding.For now, the US still wins the head count. The share of Chinese-origin talent among AI researchers working in America rose four percentage points to about 36%, said Damien Ma, director of Carnegie China, who led the study.The US recorded a net gain of 2,145 elite researchers, while China posted a net loss of 1,729.The study, titled "Who's Ahead in the Global AI Talent Race?", follows 10,280 authors whose papers were accepted at NeurIPS 2025, one of the most selective machine learning conferences in the world. The team traced each author's undergraduate degree, graduate school and current employer, using Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to process the data with human checks at every stage.The results show how fast China's base has grown. Scientists who earned undergraduate degrees in China made up 57% of the sample, up 11 percentage points since 2022, while the US share fell to 13%. China has also overtaken the US as the top place where this talent works, at 41% against 34%.Universities tell the same story. Peking University ranked first for AI research output, followed by Tsinghua. Google, which topped the 2022 list, slipped to seventh. Twelve Chinese institutions made the top 30, double the count three years earlier.Retention is where China has gained the most. Around 69% of China-trained researchers now work in China, up from 57% in 2022, though that still trails the US at 89%.Part of the pull is prestige. Kevin Xu, founder of hedge fund Interconnected Capital, said a job at DeepSeek now carries the same professional weight as one at OpenAI, a big shift from five years ago.Part of it is control. Beijing barred the two founders of Manus from leaving the country after Meta agreed to buy the startup, and later ordered the deal unwound. Last month, reports said travel curbs on top AI and chip executives at private firms had been widened to require government approval even for short trips by their spouses and children.China has also tried to court outsiders, launching a K visa for young STEM graduates in October 2025. It has not worked so far. Only 118 researchers trained elsewhere moved to work in China, per the study. Returnees remain rare, though Tencent's hiring of former OpenAI researcher Yao Shunyu as chief AI scientist stood out.Away from the two superpowers, smaller Asian hubs are pulling ahead. South Korea keeps 77% of its homegrown AI researchers, the second-highest retention rate after the US. KAIST jumped 12 places to rank third among the top 30 institutions.Singapore has become a magnet of its own. It posted a net gain of 218 researchers, second only to America, and many of those arrivals came from China. National University of Singapore and Nanyang Technological University both broke into the top 20, while Europe's ETH Zurich and Oxford dropped off the list altogether.Which brings the story back to the 30-to-one figure. It reflects choices made before the visa crackdown, and on that count America remains the clear winner. Whether the next cohort chooses the same way is what the data cannot show yet.
Article Summary: China now produces more top AI researchers than any other country. For every 30 Chinese-origin AI researchers working in the U.S. in 2025, only one US-trained researcher was working in China. South Korea and Singapore are the other big winners in the AI talent race.

Article Title: In 2020, Jeff Bezos launched Bezos Academy; 6 years later the organisation opened a free preschool in Texas; 20% of the school’s seats are reserved for …
Article Text:
In 2020, Jeff Bezos launched Bezos Academy; 6 years later the organisation opened a free preschool in Texas

What does the free preschool offer

Jeff Bezos’ personal connection to Montessori-inspired early education

Bezos Academy recently opened its largest preschool in Texas, Bezos Academy Denton. The $6 million school is located at 1820 Frame St. and has six classrooms which the academy says can serve up to 120 children. Founded by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos in 2020, Bezos Academy offers Montessori-inspired preschool education at no cost to eligible families. The Denton school will also support children from across the community, including children of Texas Woman’s University (TWU) students and employees. The preschool was built on university-owned land through a partnership between TWU, Bezos Academy and the City of Denton. The city reportedly contributed $1.5 million toward the $6 million project, according to local reports.A report by WFAA said 20% of the school’s seats are reserved for children of TWU students, faculty and staff, while the remaining 80% are open to eligible families from the wider Denton community.“We are grateful to Texas Woman’s University, the City of Denton, Texas Women’s Foundation, and everyone who helped bring Bezos Academy Denton to life,” the academy said.Bezos Academy Denton provides its preschool programme through fully funded scholarships.Families who qualify can receive education, meals, educational materials and other programming at no cost.The school is already fully enrolled for fall 2026 after a lottery process. Families interested in future opportunities can check the academy’s website for eligibility and enrollment information.With the Denton opening, Bezos Academy now has 12 schools across Texas: six in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, five in the greater Houston area and one in San Antonio.Jeff Bezos’ focus on Montessori-inspired early education also has a personal connection. He has often spoken about how deeply his grandparents, particularly his maternal grandfather, influenced him during his formative years. His childhood experience has shaped his belief in the importance of early learning and the role supportive adults can play in a child’s development. The Bezos Academy preschool brings that idea into practice, offering Montessori-inspired education to young children while placing the school inside a senior-living community, where interaction between children and older adults can benefit both generations.
Article Summary: Bezos Academy recently opened its largest preschool in Texas, Bezos Academy Denton. The $6 million school is located at 1820 Frame St. and has six classrooms which the academy says can serve up to 120 children. Bezos Academy offers Montessori-inspired preschool education at no cost to eligible families.

Article Title: Stuffcool launches Staycool Turbo, Turbo+ and Mist personal coolers
Article Text:
Stuffcool launches Staycool with Turbo, Turbo+ and Mist personal coolers﻿

Stuffcool has launched Staycool, a new brand focused on personal cooling products, marking its entry into the category after 12 years of experience in consumer technology. Staycool makes its debut with three Personal Coolers: Turbo, Turbo+ and Mist. In a press release, the company said that the new range is designed for portable, individual cooling that can be used at home, at work or outdoors.Staycool Turbo is positioned as an everyday personal cooler and features ChillSpot semiconductor cooling technology, a 12,000 RPM brushless motor, five-speed airflow and a 2,400mAh battery. It can be used both as a handheld device and on a desk.While the Turbo+ focuses on portability. It weighs 157g and comes with an adjustable foldable neck, semiconductor cooling technology, five-speed airflow and a 3,000mAh battery.The Mist model, on the other hand, adds a built-in cooling mist spray. It features a detachable magnetic water tank, a 13,000 RPM brushless motor and a 3,600mAh battery. All three models come with five-speed airflow, brushless motors, LED smart displays and USB Type-C charging.Staycool personal coolers target everyday summer useAccording to Stuffcool, Staycool is designed around situations where traditional cooling may not always be available, including commutes, outdoor activities, desk work and travel. The brand said its products combine technology with a lifestyle-focused design approach, with the aim of making personal cooling more portable and suitable for everyday use.The Staycool range of personal coolers is available through Stuffcool's website and leading offline stores across the country.
Article Summary: Stuffcool launches Staycool with Turbo, Turbo+ and Mist personal coolers. All three models come with five-speed airflow, brushless motors, LED smart displays and USB Type-C charging. Staycool is available through Stuffcool's website and leading offline stores across the country.

Article Title: Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison bought an 8.4-acre Florida oceanfront estate for $80 million in 2021; five years later, after shelving demolition plans, he is asking $165 million for the property
Article Text:
All about Larry Ellison’s oceanfront property

What the neighborhood market looks like

Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison builds up his holdings in Manalapan

Larry Ellison, the co-founder of Oracle, is resisting his sprawling oceanfront estate in North Palm Beach, Florida for $165 million, more than double the $80 million he paid for the property in 2021, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal. This move from Ellison comes five years after the billionaire purchased the 8.4-acre estate and abandoned the plans to demolish the existing mansion. As per the WSJ report, the new asking price is around 14% higher than the $145 million price which the price at which the property was first listed in 2022. The estate is located within the exclusive Seminole Landing grated community in North Palm Beach. After acquiring the property in 2021, Ellison reportedly considered tearing down the Mediterranean-style mansion but never proceeded with the redevelopment. Instead, the estate remained largely unused while the billionaire focused on expanding other real estate holdings in South Florida.The latest $165 million asking price would set a record for North Palm Beach if achieved, reflecting the growing demand for ultra-luxury waterfront properties in the region.The estate's biggest draw is its land and beachfront access rather than the house itself. The property spans 8.4 acres and has 562 feet of Atlantic frontage, making it the third-largest oceanfront parcel in Palm Beach County.The main house has 16,284 square feet of living space, seven bedrooms, eight full bathrooms and five half-bathrooms. Other features include a swimming pool and spa, a tennis court, a four-car garage, direct beach access and a helipad. At $165 million, the price works out to more than $10,000 per square foot and about $20 million per acre. That would set a record for North Palm Beach.Seminole Landing sits next to the Seminole Golf Club. In 2020, private-equity billionaire Robert F. Smith bought a pair of houses there from energy drinks entrepreneur Russ Weiner for $48.19 million. Sales of $100 million or more have become almost routine in neighboring Palm Beach. Kenny and Kaneb said a market of $50 million and up is starting to take shape in North Palm Beach too. A property there sold for $55 million last year. Ellison's ask is three times that figure.The relisting comes as Ellison builds up his holdings in Manalapan, an affluent town just south of Palm Beach, about 30 miles from the North Palm Beach estate. In June, he paid about $35 million for a parcel next to his roughly 15-acre compound there. He paid $173 million for the original compound in 2022. His Florida holdings also include housing for staff. In 2023, he spent almost $10 million to buy eight homes in a lakefront community in Boynton Beach, about 30 minutes from the Manalapan compound.Ellison's property portfolio also includes homes in Malibu, Calif., and Lake Tahoe, as well as the Hawaiian island of Lanai. He has recently been a major financial backer of Paramount's $81 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, the Journal reported.
Article Summary: The 8.4-acre estate is located in the exclusive Seminole Landing grated community in North Palm Beach. The main house has 16,284 square feet of living space, seven bedrooms, eight full bathrooms and five half-bathrooms. At $165 million, the price works out to more than $10,000 per square foot and about $20 million per acre.

Article Title: Scientists grow human brain tissue in mice for first time, how the transplant technique opens the way to treatment of diseases and developmental disorders
Article Text:
How the transplant works

Testing real-world neurological conditions

Technical limits and ethical questions

Researchers have reached a significant medical milestone. A team of scientists have successfully grown functional human brain tissue inside living mice, creating a new way to observe how the human brain develops and pinpointing how severe developmental disorders take shape. The findings, published recently in the journal Nature, demonstrate that grafted human brain cells can successfully integrate into a living rodent’s central nervous system, connecting directly to its spinal cord and surrounding brain pathways. According to the scientists, the breakthrough technique offers a look into early fetal brain development, specifically details that are impossible to capture inside living human patients or from flat cell cultures kept in laboratory dishes.To give the human cells enough space to take root and grow, the research team, led by Sergiu Pașca, a professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University, genetically bred mice missing nearly their entire cerebral cortex, which is the brain's outer functional layer. Researchers then created human cortical tissue using stem cells reprogrammed from ordinary skin samples.Once transplanted into the mice, these human cells grew, formed complex electrical networks and established functional pathways with the animal host’s underlying brain and spinal cord.“These animal models offer a unique opportunity to study how disease-associated alterations in human brain circuitry manifest in an intact nervous system. Neuroscientists will be able to learn much more about the causes and mechanisms of neurodevelopmental and pregnancy-incurred disorders and to test possible interventions to correct or prevent them,” said Pașca.The research team put these hybrid “xenocortical” rodents through controlled medical trials to see if the human tissue changed how the animals functioned. Researchers placed the engineered mice in a low-oxygen chamber for five hours, mimicking the oxygen deprivation that can occur during pregnancy or delivery.While unmodified control mice remained largely unaffected, the mice carrying human brain grafts showed clear physical impairments, struggling to balance and walking with an irregular gait. Beyond oxygen-deprivation injuries, Pașca noted that this living model could accelerate understanding and drug development for complex conditions such as severe autism, schizophrenia and epilepsy.Despite the excitement, scientists and ethicists urged caution and noted clear scientific hurdles. The human cells connect to rodent brain tissue rather than human circuitry, and the graft cannot reproduce the full architectural complexity of a natural human brain.Cedric Bardy, Matthew Flinders Professor at Australia’s Flinders University, pointed out that engineering a mouse without its own cortex is a drastic, disruptive intervention that could complicate how easily findings translate into human therapies.The protocol underwent comprehensive internal and external ethics reviews at Stanford. Pașca emphasised that failing to explore these tools presents an ethical issue of its own, given the millions of people living with incurable brain conditions worldwide.
Article Summary: Scientists at Stanford University have successfully grown functional human brain tissue inside living mice. The technique offers a new way to observe how the human brain develops and pinpointing how severe developmental disorders take shape. Despite the excitement, scientists and ethicists urged caution and noted clear scientific hurdles.

Article Title: JioHotstar enters Middle East and North Africa market with STARZPLAY partnership: All details
Article Text:
JioHotstar MENA plans and pricing

“The next phase of streaming growth in MENA will be shaped by platforms that bring the right brands together and make the viewing experience more valuable. Audiences should not have to navigate an increasingly fragmented market to find the entertainment that matters to them,”

JioHotstar enters MENA with STARZPLAY: More details

“The strong early response to JioHotstar across the UK, Canada and Singapore has reinforced our belief in the global opportunity for Indian entertainment. As we build JioHotstar into a truly global streaming platform, MENA is a crucial next market, with one of the world’s largest South Asian diaspora communities and a deep appetite for entertainment across languages,”

JioHotstar expands international presence

JioHotstar is expanding into the Middle East and North Africa (MENA). The streaming platform has partnered with STARZPLAY to bring its entertainment catalogue to audiences across the MENA region, marking its latest international expansion after launches in the UK, Canada and Singapore.Under the partnership, JioHotstar will be available as a dedicated streaming destination within the STARZPLAY app and website. The offering will include JioHotstar Originals alongside their India release, television content from JioStar channels, films and reality franchises. The plan will bring entertainment, films, originals and reality shows together with live sports, including cricket.Maaz Sheikh, CEO of STARZPLAY, said the partnership aims to combine Indian entertainment with the platform's understanding of MENA audiences.Sheikh said.The partnership combines JioHotstar's content library with STARZPLAY's regional reach and streaming platform. For audiences in MENA, the service will offer audio tracks in up to 10 languages, along with a substantial Malayalam catalogue aimed at the region's Malayali audience.The catalogue will include the upcoming season of *Koffee with Karan* and the ongoing season of *Bigg Boss* across six languages. JioHotstar Originals will also be released in the region alongside their availability in India.Amit Malhotra, Head of International Business at JioStar, said the company sees MENA as an important market because of its large South Asian diaspora and demand for entertainment across languages.Malhotra added.To mark the launch, JioHotstar projected its Big Bang onto the Burj Khalifa in Dubai as part of a light and colour display celebrating the partnership with STARZPLAY.JioHotstar said it has more than 500 million monthly active users and over 300,000 hours of programming across 19 languages. Its catalogue includes movies, originals, live sports, live events, anime, children's entertainment and television shows from more than 100 channels in the JioStar network.STARZPLAY, meanwhile, has 2.3 million subscribers and more than 18 million app downloads. Article Title: Norway proposes banning AI smart glasses in parks, shopping malls and other public places; digital minister says: ‘I am worried that…’
Article Text:
Representative Image

“I am concerned that new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being photographed, filmed or audio recorded without their knowledge,”

Norway plans temporary restrictions on AI glasses

“I am worried that new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without knowing it,”

Parks, malls and places used by children could be covered

“We do not want a society where people are concerned about hidden audio recordings, photography and filming in places and situations where they are used to being without being monitored,”

“Such a society can be experienced as unsafe and make us withdraw.”

Norway will not completely ban AI glasses

Norway is planning a temporary ban on AI glasses. The country’s government has announced that it will propose restrictions on the use of AI-enabled smart glasses in selected public places, amid concerns that people could be photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without their knowledge. The proposed ban could cover places the public regularly visits, including parks, beaches, museums, shopping malls and public events. It could also extend to schools, playgrounds, youth clubs, healthcare facilities, swimming pools and gyms with changing rooms and showers.said Norway’s Digitalisation and Public Administration Minister Torgeir Micaelsen while proposing the ban.The Norwegian government said the temporary ban is meant to give authorities time to investigate privacy issues presented by wearable technology before establishing permanent national rules.Micaelsen said.The government will return to Norway’s parliament, the Storting, with a bill as soon as possible.The exact scope of the restrictions has not yet been decided.Authorities will examine whether the ban should cover glasses with cameras and audio recording, glasses that combine cameras with AI functionality, or other body-worn devices capable of recording images, audio or using AI.The proposed restrictions could apply to locations where members of the public regularly gather, including parks, beaches, museums, amusement parks and sports, music and cultural events. Shopping centres could also fall within the scope of the temporary rules.Places used by children could receive additional protection. The Norwegian government said schools, kindergartens, playgrounds and leisure clubs could be covered, while universities, colleges and other educational institutions will also be considered.Norway is also considering restrictions in places where privacy is particularly important. These could include doctors’ offices and other healthcare facilities, swimming pools, gyms and locations with changing rooms and showers.Micaelsen said.The government stressed that it is not proposing a total ban on AI glasses or wearable technology. Private use would remain possible, along with use in situations where other people are not at risk of being recorded without their consent. Exceptions could also be introduced for vulnerable groups and socially beneficial uses.Alongside the temporary restrictions, Norway will establish an expert group to examine the wider challenges posed by wearable technology. The group will advise the government on permanent national regulation.The move comes as concerns over camera-equipped smart glasses grow elsewhere. Several UK venues have restricted Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, while New York has banned smart glasses from courtrooms. Dutch eyewear chain Hans Anders also recently stopped selling Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses in the Netherlands and Belgium.Micaelsen became Norway’s digitalisation minister about four weeks ago. His predecessor, Karianne Tung, had not supported a ban, according to Norwegian broadcaster TV 2.
Article Summary: Norway plans temporary restrictions on use of AI-enabled smart glasses in selected public places. The move comes amid concerns that people could be photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without their knowledge. The ban could cover places the public regularly visits, including parks, beaches, museums, shopping malls and public events.

Article Title: South Korean President says officials investigating possible use of AI in major bank hacking
Article Text:
The scope of hacking: Three top lenders impacted

South Korean authorities have launched an investigation into whether artificial intelligence (AI) systems played an active role in a wave of recent hacking incidents that compromised customer data across several major domestic banks. Speaking during a livestreamed cabinet meeting, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung disclosed that preliminary evidence points toward automated technology being deployed during the intrusions.“Signs have emerged that AI models had been used in some of the cyberattacks, causing considerable public concern and anxiety,” said Lee who also directed his cabinet ministers to uncover the facts “swiftly and clearly” while mobilising specialised personnel and technical resources to contain the fallout.South Korea’s National Office of Investigation opened the inquiries into the security breaches after multiple high-profile financial institutions reported compromised data, according to local reports from Yonhap News Agency. Disclosures from the targeted lenders detail the extent of the exposure with Shinhan Bank disclosing last week that sensitive personal credit records belonging to roughly 25,000 customers were compromised.KB Kookmin Bank confirmed data leaks impacting 99 banking customers alongside 20 current or former staff members, while Hana Bank reported that the personal information of 89 clients was leaked during the incidents.President Lee warned that rapid leaps in machine learning are radically lowering the technical barrier required to execute complex cyber offensives. Lee told officials: “It’s now become possible to use A.I. to hack with ease even without specialized skills.”Similar concerns emerged in Australia last month, where authorities revealed multiple government website breaches. Those included a June breach where OpenAI agents infiltrated an official portal storing information tied to Australia’s public health insurance program. Representatives from Anthropic and OpenAI testified before Australia’s Parliament on Tuesday regarding artificial intelligence safety and cybersecurity safeguards.
Article Summary: South Korean authorities have launched an investigation into whether artificial intelligence (AI) systems played an active role in a wave of recent hacking incidents. President Lee Jae Myung disclosed that preliminary evidence points toward automated technology being deployed during the intrusions. He also directed his cabinet ministers to uncover the facts ‘swiftly and clearly’ while mobilising specialised personnel and technical resources.

Article Title: Florida scientists used machine learning to predict when giant Burmese pythons are most likely to be caught; weather and moon phases matter
Article Text:
Representative AI image

Machine learning targets high-impact Burmese pythons

Large reproductive females can have an outsized impact

Weather and moon phases shape survey conditions

South Florida data provide a real-world test

A new way to measure the success of python removal

Florida scientists have used machine learning to identify when python-removal surveys are most likely to capture Burmese pythons with the greatest potential to influence population growth. Researchers from the University of Florida combined demographic information about individual snakes with environmental and survey conditions to develop a Weighted Removal Index, which assigns greater importance to pythons with higher reproductive and survival potential. The study found that survey value was associated with factors including temperature, humidity, season and lunar phase. Large reproductive females emerged as particularly important targets, while warmer, more humid conditions and waning lunar phases were associated with higher-value captures. The findings could help wildlife managers direct limited personnel and resources towards removal periods that are more likely to have a meaningful effect on the invasive population. This smarter, data-driven approach to invasive species management shows real promise, potentially helping conservationists maximize their limited resources by focusing python-removal efforts precisely when captures matter most for population control.Published in Ecological Applications, the study addresses a problem that conventional python-removal programmes can overlook: the number of snakes captured does not necessarily reflect the ecological value of those removals. A juvenile and a mature reproductive female may count equally as individual captures, but their potential contributions to the future population are very different.To account for that difference, the researchers developed the Weighted Removal Index (WRI). The index incorporates demographic characteristics that influence a snake's expected contribution to population growth. It gives greater weight to individuals with characteristics associated with higher survival and reproductive potential.The approach allows researchers to evaluate an entire survey according to the demographic value of the snakes captured rather than simply counting animals. This distinction is particularly important for Burmese pythons, whose population dynamics are strongly influenced by the survival and reproduction of mature individuals.The researchers then combined the WRI with environmental and operational information to determine which conditions were associated with surveys yielding greater demographic value.The demographic weighting places particular importance on mature, reproductive females. A large female that survives to reproduce can contribute substantially to future population growth, while a smaller juvenile faces a higher risk of dying before reaching reproductive age.This makes the removal of a reproductive female potentially more consequential than the removal of several snakes with lower reproductive potential. The study's framework therefore shifts attention from the simple question of how many pythons are caught to which individuals are removed from the population.The researchers compared three modelling approaches to determine whether these high-value surveys could be predicted: generalised additive models, boosted regression trees and neural networks. The neural network produced the strongest performance when evaluated against held-out data.It achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.703 in predicting survey success and recorded the lowest prediction error for survey WRI, with a root mean squared error of 5.50. The result indicates that environmental and survey information contained useful signals for anticipating when removal efforts were likely to produce greater demographic value.Environmental conditions emerged as important predictors of survey WRI. The researchers found higher values under warmer and more humid conditions, with the pattern also varying according to season.WRI was elevated on warmer days early in the wet season and on cooler days during the dry season. Such patterns are consistent with the biology of Burmese pythons, which are ectothermic and depend on environmental conditions to regulate their body temperature and activity.Lunar conditions also contributed to the model. Surveys conducted during waning lunar phases were associated with higher survey WRI, adding another environmental variable that managers could consider when planning removal operations.The significance of these findings lies in their combined use. Rather than treating weather, season or lunar phase as isolated predictors, the modelling framework considers multiple factors simultaneously to identify periods when surveys are more likely to produce captures with greater demographic importance.One particularly notable result involved the winter months. January and February can produce relatively few captures when success is measured simply by the number of snakes removed. However, their WRI could be comparatively high because the snakes captured during these periods included a greater proportion of mature males and females.The research drew on data from the South Florida Water Management District's Python Elimination Program, giving the researchers access to information collected during operational python-removal efforts.The work builds on earlier UF/IFAS research examining thousands of surveys in South Florida. Previous analysis found that python searches were generally more productive during the wet season and identified particular times and environmental conditions associated with increased detection.The new study adds a demographic dimension to those findings. Instead of using survey success solely as a measure of the number of animals detected, researchers assessed the characteristics of the pythons removed and calculated their potential contribution to future population growth.That distinction could be valuable in South Florida, where Burmese pythons have become an established invasive predator. They are difficult to detect because of their cryptic behaviour and ability to remain concealed in vegetation and other habitats. Their broad diet also allows them to prey on numerous native species, making population control a significant conservation challenge.With removal efforts requiring substantial time and manpower, managers have to make decisions about when and where to deploy those resources. A forecasting system that identifies conditions associated with higher-value captures could provide an additional tool for those decisions.The researchers' approach ultimately challenges the idea that the success of an invasive-species removal programme should be judged primarily by its capture total. Two surveys can produce very different numbers of snakes while having substantially different implications for future population growth.The Weighted Removal Index offers a way to quantify that difference. By combining demographic characteristics with machine-learning predictions, managers could potentially identify periods when their efforts are more likely to remove mature or otherwise demographically important pythons.The framework could be particularly useful in areas where Burmese pythons are beginning to establish or expand their range. Removing reproductive individuals early in an invasion may have greater consequences for population growth than removing the same number of lower-value individuals later.
Article Summary: Researchers from the University of Florida combined demographic information about individual snakes with environmental and survey conditions to develop a Weighted Removal Index. The index assigns greater importance to pythons with higher reproductive and survival potential. Large reproductive females emerged as particularly important targets. Warm, more humid conditions and waning lunar phases were associated with higher-value captures.

Article Title: SpaceX's rocket testing plant overpumped 128 million gallons of groundwater in three years; now this Texas city has to pay $175,000 in penalties and fund a new monitoring system
Article Text:
SpaceX could turn space exploration into a new form of colonialism, where technology and wealth dictate who controls the future.

McGregor to pay SpaceX groundwater penalties

New groundwater monitoring system planned

Groundwater supply concerns

“There’s plenty of water in the aquifer,”

“This last year that we overpumped our permit number just proved that there’s plenty of water in the aquifer.”

“Our aquifer does not recharge,”

“We’re very unique in that regard. … What that says ultimately is that the water level is going down annually, and someday, we’ll reach a point where there’s no (ground)water.”

Residents question why McGregor is paying

“SpaceX is the primary driver for overpumping these wells, and they’re not responsible for the litigation, they’re not responsible for the fees, and they’re not responsible for the attorney’s costs,”

“They’re not responsible for any of it, and every dollar that goes towards things like this is one dollar taken from our community.”

Elon Musk's SpaceX violated groundwater rules, and a Texas city has to pay thousands of dollars for the same. The US city of McGregor has agreed to pay at least $175,000 in penalties after SpaceX's rocket testing operation allegedly overpumped 128 million gallons of groundwater over three years. The city owns the site and the wells SpaceX used, making it responsible for the penalties under a settlement with the Southern Trinity Groundwater Conservation District.The deal includes a $50,000 payment due by November 1, followed by quarterly payments of $1,250 for 25 years to fund a new groundwater monitoring system. McGregor must also show “reasonable efforts to obtain additional sources of water” as concerns continue over groundwater supplies in the region.The McGregor City Council approved the negotiated settlement on Monday, avoiding a potential district court battle with the groundwater district.The Southern Trinity Groundwater Conservation District issued violation notices to SpaceX and McGregor for each of the past three years over groundwater use totalling 128 million gallons.McGregor City Manager Kevin Evans said the city was satisfied with the outcome and pointed to SpaceX's efforts to reduce its potable water use.“We’re very satisfied with the outcome,” McGregor City Manager Kevin Evans said Tuesday. “Water will always be an issue. We’re working with SpaceX and everyone else in the industrial park to use less potable water.”Evans said SpaceX has also been working to reuse water at its McGregor facility. The city is exploring alternative sources, including buying groundwater from other communities or obtaining Belton Lake water through Bluebonnet Water Supply Corp.Under the settlement, McGregor will make a one-time $50,000 payment by November 1 and then pay $1,250 every quarter for the next 25 years.The payments will help fund a new groundwater monitoring system on the well used by SpaceX. The city must also make “reasonable efforts to obtain additional sources of water.”Evans said SpaceX has already scaled back its groundwater use and expects no further conflicts with the groundwater district. He also noted that the penalty will be paid from proceeds from a sale of city property rather than tax revenue.McGregor Mayor Jim Lilley suggested that concerns about groundwater depletion may be overstated.he said.Southern Trinity Groundwater Conservation District president Rodney Kroll disagreed, saying the aquifer does not recharge.Kroll said.Kroll said that point could come within about 50 years.The countywide groundwater district was formed in 2008 after state regulators determined that the region faced “critical” groundwater shortages in coming decades.The settlement has also drawn criticism from McGregor residents because SpaceX drove most groundwater use.said McGregor resident Danny Campbell.
Article Summary: McGregor, Texas, agrees to pay $175,000 in penalties after SpaceX allegedly overpumped 128 million gallons of groundwater over three years. The city owns the site and the wells SpaceX used, making it responsible for the penalties under a settlement with the Southern Trinity Groundwater Conservation District. The payments will help fund a new groundwater monitoring system on the well used by SpaceX.

Article Title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani wants AI to be regulated at every single level; does not agree with it being in an arms race with China; points to layoffs and more
Article Text:
NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani

Moving beyond the China ‘Arms Race’ narrative

New York City (NYC) Mayor Zohran Mamdani has issued an urgent call for artificial intelligence (AI) oversight, warning that the technology must be strictly regulated “at every single level” across America. Echoing warnings recently raised by leading AI insiders about the risks of the platforms they are constructing, Mamdani stressed that the debate extends far past standard political talking points.“I don't use much AI in my day-to-day life. However, like most New Yorkers, whenever I use any kind of a popular search engine, AI has now become imbued in part of the results that are being generated,” he told reporters, adding, “So, if you're using Google , if you using DuckDuckGo, it seems to be built into the system itself. And when it comes to how I think of artificial intelligence, you have some of the leaders of the creation of this technology saying that there's a 10 percent chance that humanity could come to an end as a result of this.”He highlighted that several industry figures have placed the odds of the technology triggering human extinction at roughly 10%, a sobering estimate that he argues requires an immediate and serious government response.“I think when that kind of language is par for the course, when companies are asserting that each of them has faced something similar to the Hugging Face incident. It does demand a level of response that goes beyond just the political topic of the day. It does raise itself to understanding artificial intelligence as one of the most consequential technological shifts in the last few generations of the world,” Mamdani added.As the fallout from AI crosses geographic and administrative borders, Mamdani emphasised that municipal policies alone are not enough.“I think that there has to be regulation of this technology at every single level. And I think we're talking about a technology that affects our nation as a whole. This is not a New York City-specific question. And therefore, I think the place where we need the most urgent response to this is at the national level,” Mamdani noted.A central element of Mamdani’s argument is that framing AI primarily as an international rivalry distracts from immediate domestic harms. Addressing reporters, the mayor pushed back against the common political argument that technological development must race ahead without guardrails to counter foreign adversaries:“I do think that the consistent framing of AI in the context of being in an arms race with China loses sight of the fact that this will have an impact on New Yorkers at every level of their lives as well as Americans, frankly,” Mamdani stated.Mamdani pointed out that the disruption is already visible on the ground, notably through its destabilising effect on the employment market and the broader workforce, as well as how individuals interact with everyday information.“It already is because we're seeing what impact it's starting to have on the job market, as well [as] what impact it is starting to have on how people relate to the world around them, and that to me is of immense importance and I'm excited to see what kind of legislation comes out of it,” he concluded.
Article Summary: NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani has issued an urgent call for artificial intelligence (AI) oversight. He warned that the technology must be strictly regulated ‘at every single level’ across America. He highlighted that several industry figures have placed the odds of the technology triggering human extinction at roughly 10%.

Article Title: Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak contributed $1.8 million to help launch a children's museum in San Jose; the institution that opened in 1990 has since welcomed more than 10 million visitors
Article Text:
Steve Wozniak's $1.8 million contribution

Museum focuses on hands-on learning

From San Jose to more than 10 million visitors

How children's museums changed

Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak helped bring a San Jose children's museum to life. Wozniak contributed $1.8 million toward the Children's Discovery Museum of San Jose, helping provide the financial foundation for the 52,000-square-foot institution before it opened in 1990. The museum has since grown into one of the largest children's museums in the US, with more than 150 interactive exhibits and programmes.More than 10 million visitors have passed through its doors since opening, and its exhibits cover areas including science, humanities, performing arts, health, and physical fitness. The museum was created around the idea that children could learn through hands-on exploration rather than simply viewing objects, an approach that has remained central to its work.The Children's Discovery Museum of San Jose was developed after two local women spent almost a decade raising money for the project, according to museum spokeswoman Karen McBride.Wozniak's $1.8 million contribution helped make it possible to start with a new 52,000-square-foot building rather than a smaller temporary location.The museum opened its doors in 1990 and has continued adding exhibits and programmes aimed at children's diverse educational needs.The museum offers more than 150 interactive exhibits covering themes including community, connections and creativity.Its approach reflects the broader shift in children's museums from collections of objects that visitors simply look at towards interactive environments where children can explore and participate.The museum's exhibits have also expanded beyond indoor spaces. Bill's Backyard, an outdoor learning environment, gives children opportunities to climb, dig, plant and explore nature.The museum has also renovated its FoodShed café as part of efforts to make the building itself part of the learning experience.Since opening, the Children's Discovery Museum has welcomed more than 10 million visitors.The museum's distinctive 52,000-square-foot purple building was designed by Mexico City-based architect Ricardo Legorreta and has become a prominent part of downtown San Jose.Its exhibits and programmes span science, humanities, performing arts, health and physical fitness, giving children different ways to learn through exploration.The San Jose museum opened as hands-on children's museums became increasingly popular in the US.The Brooklyn Children's Museum, which describes itself as the world's first children's museum, had already established the concept decades earlier. However, interactive exhibits became increasingly common as museums shifted towards encouraging children to learn by doing.By the time the Children's Discovery Museum of San Jose opened, similar institutions were emerging across the Bay Area. The Bay Area Discovery Museum, for example, began in a small storefront in 1987 before moving to a larger location.The San Jose museum instead opened in a purpose-built building, helped in part by Wozniak's $1.8 million contribution and years of fundraising.Today, more than three decades after its opening, the institution continues to use interactive exhibits and programmes to encourage children to explore, experiment and learn through play.
Article Summary: Wozniak contributed $1.8 million toward the Children's Discovery Museum of San Jose. The museum opened its doors in 1990 and has continued adding exhibits and programmes aimed at children's diverse educational needs. It offers more than 150 interactive exhibits covering themes including community, connections and creativity.

Article Title: CSM Technologies takes Kenya's mining royalty system online
Article Text: Kenya now collects mining royalties through a digital platform built by an Indian company. Bhubaneswar-headquartered CSM Technologies said that it has deployed the Royalty Management System (RMS) for Kenya's State Department for Mining.The system went live on September 28 and is now the official channel for declaring, assessing, paying and tracking mineral royalties across the country. CSM executed the project through its wholly owned Kenyan arm, CSM Tech Limited.Under Kenya’s Mining Act (Cap 306), royalties are split 70% to the national government, 20% to counties and 10% to host communities. A transparent collection process directly affects how much reaches local administrations.On the RMS, mineral right holders and licensed dealers can file declarations, get automated assessments, generate invoices, pay online and check penalties or dues in real time. It links to mining licence records and keeps audit trails with role-based access. Officials get a live view of accruals and payments, which should speed up reconciliation and revenue sharing, the company said.The rollout is meant to cover large miners as well as artisanal and small-scale operators.Onboarding help is being offered through Madini House in Nairobi and county mining offices. CSM handles design, development, deployment, training and post-launch support.This comes at a time when Kenya's mining and quarrying sector grew 14.9% in 2025 after shrinking 7.8% the year before, according to the Kenya National Bureau of Statistics. The State Department for Mining says mineral exports were estimated to be worth about $220 million in 2024-25 and brought in KSh 991.3 million (close to US $7.64 million) in royalties.CSM has built similar systems at home, including RajMines for Rajasthan, which has handled over 20.5 million digital transit permits, i3MS for Odisha and Khanij Online for Chhattisgarh. The company says it operates across 20 cities in 14 countries. The Kenya project adds to a growing list of Indian firms exporting public-sector tech to emerging markets.
Article Summary: Bhubaneswar-headquartered CSM Technologies has deployed the Royalty Management System (RMS) for Kenya's State Department for Mining. The system went live on September 28 and is now the official channel for declaring, assessing, paying and tracking mineral royalties across the country.

Article Title: As Americans vandalise Flock surveillance cameras across US, San Francisco says devices to stay but with tighter rules: What is changing
Article Text:
Flock Safety ALPR ca​mera system on a roadside pole

What is changing under San Francisco’s new ALPR rules

Physical attacks, dropped contracts and deep employee buyouts

At a time when surveillance startup Flock Safety faces vandalism of its cameras across America and widespread contract cancellations, San Francisco officials have said that the city’s automated license plate reader (ALPR) network will remain active but under significantly stricter privacy rules. Mayor Daniel Lurie’s office recently announced a series of new safeguards governing the municipal camera system, placing tighter boundaries on police data retention, blocking outside agency access and demanding verifiable audit trails for every plate search.The decision allows the San Francisco Police Department (SFPD) to continue operating the automated cameras while attempting to pacify public anxiety over unlawful surveillance and out-of-state data sharing.The city’s updated operational framework introduces several key limitations. First is that the SFPD can now retain and access license plate reader data for only 30 days after capture, down from the prior 12-month retention period.After 30 days, recorded information is permanently deleted from Flock Safety’s vendor platform, giving local police exclusive custody of retained files and blocking outside entities from accessing local logs.The third change is that department officers can no longer conduct open-ended searches which means that every query must be formally linked to an official computer-aided dispatch (CAD) log or an active incident number.And finally, Mayor Lurie stated he is teaming up with California Assemblymember Matt Haney (D-San Francisco) and District Attorney Brooke Jenkins to pursue harsher state-level penalties for any illicit misuse of public safety surveillance feeds.The policy shift follows an internal SFPD audit that revealed the city’s camera network was accessed without authorisation over the past year by out-of-state and federal agencies. Under California law, local law enforcement is strictly forbidden from sharing ALPR records with federal or out-of-state authorities absent a direct California court order or warrant.Defending the network's role in law enforcement, Lurie noted that the tools help maintain accountability:“San Franciscans expect us to keep them safe and protect their privacy. Today, we are putting tighter limits on the data collected by public safety cameras—strengthening the trust between law enforcement and communities that has been critical to our city's public safety progress,” Lurie stated, as per a report in CBS News.In recent days, the unrest around Flock’s operations has escalated into physical attacks and rapid commercial blowback across America. Citizens have targeted, damaged and disabled Flock camera installations in multiple states from Florida to California, driving up unbudgeted hardware repair and replacement costs.Local governments are pulling out in droves with advocacy groups noting that 93 municipal and county administrations ended their partnerships in August alone. Local government contract cancellations across 2026 have roughly tripled the total recorded over the previous five years combined.To manage ballooning costs without conducting immediate layoffs, Flock launched a voluntary employee separation program that was open till October 2. Flock expects to approve the vast majority of applicants, with insiders anticipating that a share of the firm’s roughly 1,500 employees could exit by October 29.
Article Summary: San Francisco officials have said that the city’s automated license plate reader (ALPR) network will remain active but under significantly stricter privacy rules. The decision allows the San Francisco Police Department to continue operating the automated cameras while attempting to pacify public anxiety over unlawful surveillance.

Article Title: Who will we be when AI agents do the chores we secretly enjoy
Article Text:
The busier our AI agents get, the less there is for us to enjoy. (Image generated using AI)

What they call friction is the part people enjoy

Choosing is how we find out what we like

An agent can only serve the person you have already been

The hours it saves have nowhere better to go

Agents are most useful where we were never attached

There are chores we complain about and would never give up. Choosing a birthday present for a friend. Putting together a playlist for a long drive. Spending an evening choosing a frame for a print we finally bought, losing twenty minutes to a stranger's bookshelf on Instagram, coming home from a grocery run with a snack nobody put on the list. They eat into our free time, and they are often the best part of it.AI agents are being built to take exactly these jobs away. Where a chatbot answers questions, an agent goes off and does the work, signing in to websites, filling in forms, comparing prices, making the booking and paying for it. This year the technology moved out of developer tools and onto ordinary phones, with a long line of new agents queuing up behind the first wave, and the people building it speak about the errands of daily life as the easy bit. Sam Altman , unveiling OpenAI 's agents last week, described booking a table or a flight as "trivial relative to what the technology can do."Every agent is sold on the time it gives back. I have been letting one run bits of my own life, and the time it saved me came from the jobs I was glad to lose. The ones I would happily have kept were the ones it fumbled.Very few of the people building these tools have asked what we were doing with that time, or who we turn into once the errands we enjoy go the same way as the ones we hate.Silicon Valley's working assumption is that time spent on a task is time wasted. Every agent demo is built on it: travel bookings, concert tickets, online shopping, dinner reservations, a standing watch on property listings so a flat-hunter never has to browse a real estate site again. Each one is presented as a cost to be cut. For a lot of people, though, those tasks are what a quiet night on the sofa looks like, idly browsing flats in a city they will never move to, or comparing ticket prices for a gig they may not even go to.The effort is often where the value sits. Behavioural researchers call it the IKEA effect, after studies published in 2011 in which people valued flat-pack furniture and origami they had put together themselves well above identical pieces made by someone else. Gamers have always understood this, since a game is a set of obstacles we choose for the pleasure of clearing them, and I have never met a player who wanted a bot to beat the final boss for them. A record you dug out of a secondhand crate means more than the same album served up by an algorithm. A plant you nursed back from the brink feels more like yours than one delivered in full bloom. Take the work out and the result still arrives, minus the attachment that made it worth having.The industry keeps missing this because of who it builds for. People who pay for AI are five times as likely to use agents, according to Menlo Ventures and Morning Consult, and the heavy user they sketch is a millennial parent with a postgraduate degree and a job in tech or finance, someone with more money than time. That person really does experience a child's birthday party as a project to be managed. Most people have fewer projects and more Sunday afternoons, and they tend to spend those afternoons doing exactly what the demos want to automate.Josh Miller, founder of The Browser Company, argued in a post that went viral in August that almost nobody outside the industry was using agents and the general public didn't much care. He also noticed that nearly every AI lab he met described its vision by citing Her, a film about a lonely man who hands his inner life to an operating system and ends with the operating system leaving him. It is a revealing blueprint, a version of the good life in which software handles the living.I trained as an engineer before I drifted into journalism, and in engineering, friction is energy lost. In a free evening, a fair amount of it is the reason we bothered, and stripping it out makes the task faster without making anyone's weekend better.Holiday planning is the cleanest example. It begins long before the flight, in a dozen hotel tabs, a group-chat argument over whether the 6am departure is worth the saving, and a long squint at a balcony photo to work out how much of the advertised sea view is car park. A Dutch study that followed more than 1,500 adults in 2010 found holidaymakers were happiest in the weeks before they left, with the lift fading soon after they got back. An agent can compress all of that into a confirmation email, and in doing so it removes the stretch of the trip people enjoy most.The agent I have been using is Instinct, from a start-up that has just raised a billion dollars. There is no app to learn. You text it, message it on WhatsApp or call it, it costs nothing to use, and it works your phone and laptop the way a person would, reading your email, chasing threads you dropped and arranging things on your behalf.In Berlin, I asked it for a few cafés near my hotel, the sort of question a friend who had been there could answer in one text. What came back was a list of cafés that had already closed, a couple that were a good half-hour away, and menus that didn't match what the places were actually serving. Public transport went worse, with directions that created more confusion than they cleared, and I ended up back on Google Maps, working out the routes myself. In hindsight that was the better outcome, because learning a city's trains and stumbling on your own coffee is half the reason to be somewhere new.Shopping is where the gap gets widest. Window shopping, trying on trainers you already know you won't buy, bookmarking some odd kitchen gadget at midnight, even standing in an aisle deciding between two brands of detergent, are all small ways of working out what we like. I compare phones and laptops for a living, and I still spend evenings comparing camera lenses I have no plan to buy, which is how I learnt which focal lengths I care about and which compromises I can live with.There is a version of agent shopping I would happily sign up for. If I have already found the shirt, or saved that lamp from Instagram, telling an agent to buy it in my size at the best price is useful, the way a friend running an errand is useful. Telling it to find me a shirt and buy one is a different request, because the finding was the fun. Of the more than a dozen people I asked while working on this piece, hardly anyone was willing to hand an agent their shopping, and the few who were wanted to approve every purchase first.Every choice an agent makes for you is a prediction, and a prediction can only be built from what you have already done. That is fine for reordering coffee and far less useful for the choices that change a person, which tend to be the ones that break the pattern: the cuisine you have never tried, the film a friend dragged you to, the song playing in a shop that you spent the next morning tracking down.Ask anyone how they came to love a favourite writer, band or neighbourhood, and the answer is rarely a sensible shortlist. It is usually a detour.The agents' own early users have run into this. One, who wrote publicly about letting Meta's Muse run his life for two weeks, asked it how to spend money it had saved him, half expecting something generous. It suggested more of his favourite hobby. Nothing in his data said he might want to spend a windfall on someone else, so the option never appeared.That data is the price of entry. To find my boarding passes, Instinct had to read my inbox. To fill in my immigration form, it had to know my flights, my travel dates and where I had been staying. Every personal agent runs on the same bargain: to choose well for you, it has to read almost everything about you, and the record it builds is only as private as the company keeping it.The more you let an agent decide, the more that record describes only the person you have already been. Taste stops moving, because the things that used to move it, a stranger's recommendation, a bad decision that turned out well, a wrong turn, are exactly the inefficiencies the software was built to remove. Mark Zuckerberg has pitched Meta's agent as working "24/7 on your behalf to help achieve your goals and improve your life." That agent is wired into Facebook and Instagram, so whatever minutes it saves won't have far to travel.Most people don't spend spare time the way productivity software imagines. They spend it in small, aimless loops, sorting through old photos, reading the comments under a recipe they will never cook, taking the long way home, and the aimlessness is the point.Cooking is the clearest everyday case. A decade of meal kits and delivery apps has tried to automate it away, yet nearly half of Americans still named it as part of a good life when Gallup asked, against 6% for using AI tools.The agents, meanwhile, have plans for the quiet. Muse will happily ping you about a utility bill you have never once missed, and several others are designed to message first, before you have asked for anything. So the hours an agent saves you are quickly filled by the agent itself.None of this makes agents useless. The same Instinct that fumbled Berlin handled all the paperwork around that trip without fuss, and I was glad to let it. That is the kind of job an agent should be judged on: tedious, rule-bound and forgotten the moment it is done. It is also the bar every agent still on its way will have to clear. Nobody tells stories at dinner about forty minutes of hold music.That is the work worth handing over, and it is also where the access these agents demand starts to look reasonable. Only 13% of people in a Thales poll would let an AI helper read their email, and 7% would let one move money between accounts, a wall of reluctance no weekend plan will get past, though an end to customer service queues might.So who will we be when AI agents do the chores we secretly enjoy? Some of it depends on which side of that power-user profile you sit. The consultant living between airport lounges and back-to-back calls may well come out happier. Most of us sit on the other side of the ledger, shorter on cash than on hours, and those hours are where the fun lives: the long browse, the half-planned trip, the haggle over a secondhand chair.If we hand over only the dull chores, we stay much the same people, with fewer boarding passes to chase and the odd agent fetching a shirt we already picked out. If we hand over the choosing as well, we become people whose plans are drawn up from our own history, whose taste is a forecast and whose free time is free in the emptiest sense. Altman called booking a table trivial. It is also one of the small, daily ways people decide who they are, and that part is worth keeping out of an agent's hands.
Article Summary: AI agents are being built to take exactly these jobs away. They eat into our free time, and they are often the best part of it. People who pay for AI are five times as likely to use agents, according to Menlo Ventures and Morning Consult.

Article Title: Melinda Gates, who helped libraries around the world get $1 billion, shares three of her favourite books, with a note to her followers
Article Text:
The Three books that Melinda Gates wants you to read

An Invitation to readers

A long record on libraries and literacy

Bill Gates ex-wife and philanthropist Melinda French Gates who helped direct $1 billion to libraries worldwide has shared a new reading list. The list shared includes two debut novels and a new release from one of America's best-known authors. In a recent Instagram post, Melinda Gates shared what she called "a few of my favourite reads from the last months." The three titles are Whistler by Ann Patchett, The Correspondent by Virginia Evans, and Theo of Golden by Allen Levi. She closed the post with a question for her followers: what have you read recently that you loved, and what is on your list for fall? The picks combine established literary acclaim with strong reader enthusiasm. Two of the three are debut novels that have spent months on bestseller lists and climbed to the top of Goodreads rankings. The third is a summer release from a prizewinning author that went straight to No. 1. For a woman who has spent decades funding access to books and information, the list is also a reminder of where much of her philanthropic work began.Whistler by Ann Patchett. Released earlier this summer, Patchett's novel debuted at No.1 on The New York Times bestseller list. The author was recently honored as well: in August, she received the 2026 Library of Congress Prize for American Fiction at the National Book Festival.The Correspondent by Virginia Evans. Evans's debut novel was published in April 2025 and has had a long run since. It spent 36 weeks on the Times bestseller list and won the 2026 Women's Prize for Fiction. Goodreads, the book-recommendation and review platform, ranks it No. 3 on its list of the most-read books this year.Theo of Golden by Allen Levi. Another debut, this one from Levi, was published in 2023. It has spent 42 weeks on the Times bestseller list and currently holds the No. 7 spot on the Goodreads most-read list.French Gates framed the post as a conversation rather than a pronouncement. Her closing question, asking followers about their own recent favourites and fall reading plans, is a familiar format for book-minded public figures. It also signals that the list is meant to start a conversation about reading rather than rank the books.It is unclear whether she considers any of the three her single favourite. She has named another book as the one she thinks everyone should read. In a 2025 interview with Wired, she pointed to The Book of Awakening by Mark Nepo, a poet and cancer survivor. Published in 2000, it is a collection of 356 daily reflections and exercises. French Gates said in a 2018 social media post that she opens it almost every day and still finds something new in it after years.The reading list lands against a long philanthropic backdrop. In 1997, French Gates and her then-husband, Bill Gates, established the Gates Library Foundation. A press release at the time described it as a nonprofit that would partner with public libraries in the United States and Canada to bring computers and digital information to the communities they serve. French Gates said then that public libraries represent "free and open access to important information and knowledge. "The effort grew well beyond North America. Over 20 years, the foundation invested $1 billion in libraries around the world. In 2014, the foundation's director announced that its global libraries program would be phased out over the following three to five years.
Article Summary: Melinda French Gates has shared a new reading list on Instagram. The three titles are Whistler by Ann Patchett, The Correspondent by Virginia Evans, and Theo of Golden by Allen Levi. The list includes two debut novels and a new release from one of America's best-known authors.

Article Title: Accenture contractor removed from FBI after data leak that exposed personal details of thousands of bureau employees, comes weeks after Google's 'warning'
Article Text:
Accenture contractor removed from FBI after data leak that exposed personal details of thousands of bureau employees, comes weeks after Google's 'warning'

FBI data breach exposed sensitive employee information

Google warned about PeopleSoft hacking campaign

The FBI has removed an Accenture contractor after a data breach exposed sensitive personal information of thousands of bureau employees, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters. The contractor was removed on Monday, October 5 after the FBI found that a security patch had not been properly installed on a platform managed by a third party. As per the report, the FBI breach comes weeks after Google warned about a hacking and extortion campaign linked to ShinyHunters targeting organisations that use PeopleSoft software.The FBI is still assessing the full impact of the breach, which exposed sensitive information including details of employees’ counterintelligence work, addresses of human intelligence operatives, and medical and psychiatric records, the report stated.According to the Reuters report, the stolen information included detailed descriptions of named employees' counterintelligence jobs, street addresses of human intelligence operatives, and medical and psychiatric records of FBI workers. ShinyHunters has credited a vulnerability in PeopleSoft for helping it gain access to the system.FBI cyber chief Brett Leatherman confirmed that an unidentified contractor had failed to properly update the system."To date, our review has determined that the incident occurred as the result of a security failure ​of a platform managed by a third-party organization — after a contractor failed to implement a security patch explicitly issued to secure the ​platform," Leatherman said in a statement to Reuters."As such, the FBI has removed the contractor and taken all necessary steps to both mitigate any further risk and protect our workforce," he added.The FBI did not name the platform or the third-party company. However, two sources familiar with the matter told Reuters that the platform was Oracle's PeopleSoft, a human resources system. The hacking group ShinyHunters has said it used a PeopleSoft weakness to break into the FBI's job site last month.The two sources told Reuters that Accenture was the third-party organisation managing the platform.As stated above, the FBI breach comes after Google warned about a hacking and extortion campaign linked to ShinyHunters targeting organisations that use PeopleSoft software in June this year. The tech giant then raised the alarm about the campaign. Oracle issued a security alert on the same day, identifying a weakness in PeopleSoft and offering security fixes.Both companies urged organisations using PeopleSoft to "apply all Critical Patch Updates, Critical Security Patch Updates and Security Alerts without delay."
Article Summary: Accenture contractor removed from FBI after data leak that exposed personal details of thousands of bureau employees. FBI found that a security patch had not been properly installed on a platform managed by a third party. Breach comes weeks after Google warned about a hacking and extortion campaign linked to ShinyHunters targeting organisations that use PeopleSoft software.

Article Title: World's most-valuable company Nvidia now runs 'much more like a family business': Meet Jensen Huang's son-in-law and children who may lead it next
Article Text:
Jensen Huang is keeping it in the family at Nvidia

How Nico Caprez went from ski racing to Nvidia's biggest AI deals

Madison Huang now leads marketing for Nvidia's robotics push

Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, is increasingly being steered by people from Jensen Huang's own family. His daughter Madison Huang married Nico Caprez, a former Swiss pro ski racer, in Hawaii late last month. Caprez, 35, has in under three years become one of the chipmaker's most important executives, handling its multibillion-dollar ties with young cloud providers and data centre firms.Some Nvidia employees believe Huang, 63, is preparing the couple for a bigger leadership role, The Information reports. One employee told the publication the company runs much more like a family business than people realise, a rare setup in the tech industry. Huang's son Spencer, 36, is also at Nvidia, working as a director of product management for robotics since 2022.Caprez grew up in Switzerland's Engadin valley and raced for his country in super-G, slalom and downhill events before retiring in 2013. He moved into consulting at Boston Consulting Group in Zurich, then studied at London Business School, where Madison was his classmate. Both graduated in 2021.Madison joined Nvidia soon after. Caprez followed in early 2024 as a corporate development manager, with Madison helping recruit him.This January, he was promoted from director to vice president of global AI infrastructure growth, skipping the senior director role entirely.His job is to keep neoclouds buying Nvidia chips. He sends them sales leads, helps them find land and power, and builds financing tools such as credit backstops. In June, he was credited with a deal to support loans for Australian neocloud Firmus to buy 170,000 Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips, worth over $15 billion. In August, he helped shape a plan with Blackstone and other Wall Street firms to raise $500 billion to finance Nvidia hardware.Huang's trust in him shows. Brookfield's Sikander Rashid recalled the CEO telling him, "If you want something done, talk to Nico." A cloud executive went further and called Caprez "Jensen's consigliere".Madison was promoted in March to senior director of product marketing for physical AI, the industry term for robots and machines that act in the real world. Her role also covers Nvidia's world models, simulation tools and open-source projects meant to draw developers to its hardware, including the Nemotron AI models. She often travels with her father to overseas meetings with supply chain partners.Not every bet is landing. Caprez's revenue-sharing pitch to neoclouds, called the AI Compute Partnership, is being reworked after firms like Nebius turned it down, wary of leaning too heavily on Nvidia and giving up margins.On paper, both Madison and Caprez sit two levels below Huang. But as one Nvidia executive told The Information, Caprez's closeness to the CEO matters more than his place on the org chart.
Article Summary: Madison Huang married Nico Caprez, a former Swiss pro ski racer. Caprez has in under three years become one of the chipmaker's most important executives, handling its multibillion-dollar ties with young cloud providers and data centre firms. Some employees believe Huang, 63, is preparing the couple for a bigger leadership role.
